title: Comparison: more than
plainEnglish: It marks the thing you are comparing against, like saying than in English.
whenToUse: Use it to compare two things, often with 더 (more). Example: 기차가 버스보다 더 빨라요.
attachmentRule: Attach 보다 directly to a noun with no spacing change, after both vowels and consonants (사과보다, 물보다). The pattern is A가/는 B보다 더 Adjective.
contrastWith: 보다 marks the standard you compare to, while 처럼 means like or as (similar to), not more or less.

examples.en: My younger sibling is taller than me.
Today is colder than yesterday.
The train is faster than the bus.

examples.ko: 이 책이 저 책보다 더 재미있어요.
examples.en: This book is more interesting than that book.

commonMistakes: Putting 보다 on the wrong noun; it attaches to the standard B, not to the subject A.
Translating 더 as required everywhere; 더 is common but optional and means more.
studyOrder: Identify the two items A and B you compare
Attach 보다 to the standard B
Add 더 before the adjective for more
Finish with the adjective in 해요 form
beginnerExplanation: 보다 is how Korean says than in a comparison, and it attaches to the thing you measure against, not to the subject. Think A가 B보다 더 (adjective): in 동생이 저보다 키가 더 커요, 저 (me) is the standard, so my sibling comes out taller. In 오늘이 어제보다 더 추워요, yesterday is the standard and today is colder. The word 더 means more and usually sits right before the adjective, though you can drop it and the sentence still compares. The most common pitfall is sticking 보다 onto the subject by mistake; remember it always glues to the item you are comparing to, which in English follows the word than.

title: Optional plural marker
plainEnglish: It marks a noun as plural, but Korean usually leaves it off.
whenToUse: Use it to stress that there are many people or things, mostly with people. Example: 학생들이 교실에 있어요.
attachmentRule: Attach 들 to the end of the noun after both vowels and consonants (친구들, 학생들). With a number or counter you normally omit it (사과 세 개, not 사과들 세 개).
contrastWith: Unlike English -s, 들 is optional; a bare noun like 사과 can already mean apple or apples from context.

examples.en: The students are in the classroom.
I watch a movie together with my friends.
The children play in the park.
There are really many people.

commonMistakes: Adding 들 to every plural the way English uses -s; it is usually omitted and sounds heavy if overused.
Using 들 together with a number, like 사과들 세 개; drop 들 when a counter is present.
studyOrder: Notice Korean nouns do not need a plural mark
Add 들 only to highlight many, usually people
Attach 들 to the end of the noun
Drop 들 when a number or counter appears
beginnerExplanation: 들 turns a noun plural, but the key idea for beginners is that it is optional and Korean usually drops it. A bare noun like 사과 can mean apple or apples, and context tells you which, so you do not need 들 the way English forces -s. You see it most with people: 학생들이 교실에 있어요 (the students are in the classroom) or 친구들과 같이 가요 (I go with my friends). The main pitfall is sprinkling 들 onto everything; it sounds heavy, and you should especially leave it off when a counter is present, so say 사과 세 개 (three apples), never 사과들 세 개.

title: Counting with counters
plainEnglish: To count things you use a native number plus a counter word that matches the kind of thing.
whenToUse: Use it whenever you count objects, people, or animals. Example: 사과 두 개 주세요.
attachmentRule: Use NATIVE numbers before counters, and the numbers 1 to 4 change shape: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네 (한 개, 두 명, 세 마리). Order is noun + number + counter (사과 세 개).
contrastWith: Counters use native numbers (한, 두, 세), while dates, money, and minutes use Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼), so do not mix them.

examples.en: Two cups of coffee, please.
There are three students in the classroom.
I raise one puppy.
Two bottles of beer, please.

commonMistakes: Using Sino numbers with counters, like 이 개 instead of 두 개.
Forgetting that 1 to 4 change shape, saying 하나 개 instead of 한 개.
studyOrder: Pick the right counter: 개 things, 명 people, 마리 animals, 잔 cups, 병 bottles
Choose a native number
Change 1 to 4 to 한, 두, 세, 네 before the counter
Say it as noun + number + counter
beginnerExplanation: Korean cannot count things with a number alone; you need a counter word that matches the category, and you use native numbers in front of it. The everyday counters are 개 for objects, 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 잔 for cups or glasses, and 병 for bottles, so you say 사과 두 개 (two apples) and 학생 세 명 (three students). The big rule to memorize is that the native numbers one through four shorten before a counter: 하나 둘 셋 넷 become 한 두 세 네, giving 한 개, 두 명, 세 마리. The classic pitfall is reaching for Sino numbers like 이 or 삼; those are for dates and money, so counting people as 이 명 is wrong and you want 두 명 instead.

title: Background or soft contrast
plainEnglish: It sets up background information or a gentle but before the next clause.
whenToUse: Use it to give a situation, then add a reaction, request, or contrast. Example: 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요.
attachmentRule: For verbs and 있다/없다 add -는데 to the stem (가는데, 먹는데). For adjectives add -은데 after a consonant and -ㄴ데 after a vowel (작은데, 큰데). Past tense uses -았/었는데 (갔는데).
contrastWith: -지만 is a plain but for direct contrast, while -는데 is softer and also sets a scene or lead-in, not only contrast.

examples.en: It is raining but I do not have an umbrella.
This restaurant is tasty but a bit expensive.
I am studying now and it is very hard.
It is the weekend, so shall we watch a movie together?

commonMistakes: Using verb ending -은데 for verbs; verbs take -는데 (먹는데), and -은데 is for adjectives.
Treating -는데 as a strong but; it is softer and often just sets background for what follows.

practiceItems.prompt: it is the weekend, so (shall we watch a movie)

studyOrder: Decide if the word is a verb or an adjective
For verbs and 있다/없다 use -는데
For adjectives use -은데 or -ㄴ데
Add the reaction, request, or contrast in the next clause
beginnerExplanation: -는데 is a soft connector that paints the background first and then lets you add a reaction, a question, a request, or a light contrast. Picture giving the scene, then the point: 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요 (it is raining, and I have no umbrella) or 주말인데 같이 영화 볼래요? (it is the weekend, so shall we see a movie?). The attachment depends on word type: verbs and 있다/없다 take -는데 (가는데, 먹는데), while adjectives take -은데 after a consonant and -ㄴ데 after a vowel (작은데, 큰데). The main pitfall is mixing these up and saying 먹은데 for a verb; verbs always use -는데, and remember this ending is gentler than the blunt 지만.

title: Doing two things at once
plainEnglish: It links two actions that one person does at the same time.
whenToUse: Use it when the same subject does two actions simultaneously. Example: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요.
attachmentRule: Attach -으면서 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹으면서, 읽으면서) and -면서 to a stem ending in a vowel (가면서, 보면서). The subject of both actions must be the same person.
contrastWith: -(으)면서 means doing two things at once, while -고 just lists or sequences actions that need not overlap in time.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
I watch television while eating.
We talk while drinking coffee.
I clean while singing a song.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)면서 for two different subjects; both actions must share one subject.
Forgetting -으- after a consonant stem, saying 먹면서 instead of 먹으면서.
studyOrder: Check that one subject does both actions
Find the verb stem
Add -면서 after a vowel or -으면서 after a consonant
Put the simultaneous action in the second clause
beginnerExplanation: -(으)면서 joins two actions that one person performs at the very same time, like our word while. The rule is one subject doing both: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요 means I study while listening to music, and 밥을 먹으면서 텔레비전을 봐요 means I watch TV while eating. Attachment follows the usual vowel and consonant split: vowel-final stems take -면서 (가면서, 보면서) and consonant-final stems take -으면서 (먹으면서, 읽으면서). Two pitfalls trip up beginners: do not use it when the two clauses have different subjects, and do not drop the linking 으 after a consonant, so it is 먹으면서, never 먹면서. Compare it with -고, which only lists actions and does not force them to overlap.

title: Before doing something
plainEnglish: It says you do the main action before another action happens.
whenToUse: Use it to say before doing a verb. Example: 밥을 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요.
attachmentRule: Attach -기 전에 to any verb stem with no vowel or consonant change (먹기 전에, 가기 전에, 자기 전에). For before a noun, use Noun 전에 instead (식사 전에).
contrastWith: -기 전에 means before doing, while its opposite -(으)ㄴ 후에 means after doing; pick by which action comes first.

examples.en: I wash my hands before I eat.
I read a book before I sleep.
I turn off the light before leaving home.
I drink water before exercising.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기 전에, like 먹어기 전에; always use the plain stem plus -기 전에 (먹기 전에).
Using -기 전에 with a noun; for nouns use Noun 전에, for example 식사 전에, not 식사기 전에.

practiceItems.prompt: before going out (I turn off the light)

studyOrder: Find the action that happens later, the main verb
Take its plain dictionary stem
Add -기 전에 with no spelling change
Place the earlier event in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-기 전에 lets you say you do something before another action takes place, and it is wonderfully regular because you just add -기 전에 to the plain verb stem with no changes. Look at 밥을 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요 (I wash my hands before I eat) and 자기 전에 책을 읽어요 (I read before I sleep): the verb after 전에 is the later event, and the main clause tells what you do first. For nouns you switch to Noun 전에, as in 식사 전에 (before the meal), not 식사기 전에. The number one pitfall is conjugating the verb, writing 먹어기 전에; keep it as the bare stem 먹기. Remember its mirror image -(으)ㄴ 후에 for after, and choose based on which action comes first.

title: After doing something
plainEnglish: It says you do the main action after another action is finished.
whenToUse: Use it to say after doing a verb. Example: 밥을 먹은 후에 커피를 마셔요.
attachmentRule: Add -은 후에 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹은 후에, 읽은 후에) and -ㄴ 후에 to a stem ending in a vowel (간 후에, 본 후에). For after a noun, use Noun 후에 (식사 후에). You can replace 후에 with 다음에 or 뒤에.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄴ 후에 means after doing and uses a past-style -은/-ㄴ form, while -기 전에 means before doing and keeps the plain stem.

examples.en: I drink coffee after I eat.
I go home after class ends.
I eat after I wash my hands.
I shower after exercising.

commonMistakes: Using the plain stem like -기, saying 먹기 후에; after needs the -은/-ㄴ form, so 먹은 후에.
Forgetting the consonant and vowel split, writing 간 후에 as 가은 후에; vowel stems take -ㄴ 후에 (간 후에).
studyOrder: Find the action that happens first
Add -은 후에 after a consonant or -ㄴ 후에 after a vowel
Put the later action in the main clause
Swap 후에 for 다음에 or 뒤에 if you like
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 후에 expresses that you do the main action after another one is finished, and it pairs as the opposite of -기 전에. Unlike before, the after pattern uses the -은/-ㄴ ending: consonant stems take -은 후에 (먹은 후에, 읽은 후에) and vowel stems take -ㄴ 후에 (간 후에, 본 후에). So 밥을 먹은 후에 커피를 마셔요 means I drink coffee after eating, and 수업이 끝난 후에 집에 가요 means I go home after class ends; the verb before 후에 is the earlier event. For nouns use Noun 후에, like 식사 후에, and you may freely replace 후에 with 다음에 or 뒤에. The main pitfall is reusing the plain -기 stem from the before pattern; for after you must say 먹은 후에, not 먹기 후에.

title: Every or each
plainEnglish: It attaches to a noun to mean every or each one.
whenToUse: Use it for repeated times or each member of a group. Example: 주말마다 운동해요.
attachmentRule: Attach 마다 directly to the noun after both vowels and consonants with no change (아침마다, 주말마다, 사람마다). With time words it means every; with people or things it means each.
contrastWith: 마다 means every or each, while 매- as in 매일 or 매주 is a fixed prefix on set time words; 마다 attaches freely to many nouns.

examples.en: I exercise every weekend.
I drink coffee every morning.
Each person thinks differently.
I study Korean every day.

commonMistakes: Adding a particle after 마다 when none is needed, like 주말마다에; 마다 already carries the meaning.
Confusing 마다 with 매-; 매일 is fixed, but 마다 attaches freely, as in 주말마다.
studyOrder: Pick the noun you want to repeat or distribute
Attach 마다 directly with no spelling change
Read it as every for time words
Read it as each for people or things
beginnerExplanation: N마다 attaches to a noun and means every or each, covering both repeated times and every member of a group. With time words it lands on every: 주말마다 운동해요 (I exercise every weekend) and 아침마다 커피를 마셔요 (I drink coffee every morning). With people or things it shades toward each: 사람마다 생각이 달라요 means each person thinks differently. Attachment could not be simpler, since 마다 glues straight onto the noun after both vowels and consonants with no change. Two pitfalls: do not pile another particle on top, so avoid 주말마다에, because 마다 already does the job; and do not confuse it with the prefix 매-, which only sits on fixed words like 매일 or 매주, whereas 마다 attaches freely to almost any noun.
